text.p: THE PROTEUS COLUMN

While the immediate impact of the Credit Suisse and Winterthur merger has been widely debated, it is likely that the ripple effects will continue to spread through the global insurance industry for some time.
In Switzerland the mega-merger has already sparked speculation that Baloise, the fourth largest Swiss insurer, will soon merge with a partner or become a target for an acquisition.
Certainly analysts agree that the powerful force created by Winterthur and Credit Suisse will make it very difficult for Baloise to survive in its current form.
But the effects of the merger will also be felt further afield and a debate has begun over whether banking regulations will force Winterthur to sell off its U.S. subsidiaries.

Company officials admit that if a bill designed to rescind the U.S. Glass-Steagall Act - which prohibits affiliations between insurers and banks - fails to pass through Congress within the next four years, the disposal of Winterthur's U.S. insurance operations will be inevitable.

Although the subsidiaries are anxious to point out there is every likelihood of the bill going through, any indication that companies might be sold, especially the reinsurance companies, is likely to cause a scrum among potential buyers.

Whether or not the law requires the sell-off, some analysts are questioning how parts of Winterthur, including the U.S. operations and its Australian subsidiary HIH Winterthur, will fit into a group which is showing every sign of becoming a European retail financial services operation.
Winterthur admits that employee benefits and pensions will be among its key product areas which could represent the first signs of a shift in the balance of the company's portfolio.

There is also a distinct possibility that the merger will encourage other insurers to follow suit. Analysts say they do not expect a stream of copy-cat moves but indicate that at least one or two more mergers between banks and insurers could be predicted.

Top of the list of likely candidates, according to some analysts, would be a link between the German Dresdner Bank and Allianz. The insurer already has a 22 percent stake in Dresdner and although it has dismissed speculation of a link as "rash", a spokesman for Allianz has said the Swiss merger was a good idea.
There has also been speculation that Deutsche Bank will merge with Allianz to create a huge financial services group, although this has been denied by the bank.
The successful integration of the businesses of Credit Suisse and Winterthur is certain to be a long and difficult process with some saying it could take five years before the outcome will be known.
This in itself will be a challenge for senior management who, having come from consultancy backgrounds, may not be used to embarking on such long term projects.

They will also have to get used to the fact that a global insurance industry which is in the throes of consolidation and is also looking to form ever closer links with the banks, will be watching them every step of the way.
